title: GCSE Maths Revision for Wiltshire Students: A Practical Plan for Years 10 and 11
excerpt: A sensible way to revise GCSE Maths, identify knowledge gaps and use past papers without wasting time.

sections.heading: Start with the exact GCSE specification
paragraphs: First confirm whether the student is studying AQA, Pearson Edexcel, OCR or another awarding body, and which tier they are likely to sit. The biggest gains often come from revising skills that underpin many other topics, not simply attempting the hardest questions available.

A short topic audit can separate work the student can complete confidently from work that still needs an explanation. Use marked school assessments to identify repeated errors rather than relying on a vague feeling that Maths is difficult.

sections.heading: Revise by topic before mixing questions
paragraphs: Build a weekly routine containing a few core tasks: quick arithmetic or algebra retrieval, one focused topic, then a handful of exam-style questions. Fractions, percentages, rearranging formulae, graphs and proportional reasoning have wide application.
When a question goes wrong, record why. Did the student misread information, choose an unsuitable method, make an arithmetic slip or lack a key concept? Each of these requires a different response.

sections.heading: Use past papers as feedback, not just a score
paragraphs: Past papers are useful when students review them closely. After marking, reattempt incorrect questions with no model answer visible, then try a similar question on a later day. Under timed conditions, students also practise deciding when to move on.
For Foundation and Higher tier preparation alike, show full working and check that calculator technique is secure. A well-organised record of errors can become a personalised revision checklist.

title: How Wiltshire Families Can Choose a GCSE or A-Level Physics Tutor
excerpt: Find a Physics tutor who can explain concepts, handle the maths and teach exam technique for the correct board.

sections.heading: Physics needs concepts and calculations
paragraphs: The best Physics tutoring makes a distinction between understanding a concept and recalling an equation. Students might know an equation but struggle to identify the correct quantities, units or physical principles in an unfamiliar problem.

Ask how a tutor approaches force diagrams, electricity, energy transfers or waves. A useful explanation should include simple sketches, careful steps and questions that test whether the learner understands the reasoning.

sections.heading: Match the exam board and level
paragraphs: A-Level Physics and GCSE Physics require different levels of mathematical fluency and explanation. Confirm the exact specification, including the exam board and whether the GCSE student takes separate or combined Science.

Look for a tutor who uses current specification topics, sensible past-paper selection and the appropriate mark schemes. Where a student is struggling with the Maths behind Physics, targeted fluency practice may be just as important as additional Physics questions.

sections.heading: What to bring to the first lesson
paragraphs: Bring a recent test, the topic list, target grades and two or three questions that felt confusing. This allows the tutor to propose a useful starting point rather than delivering generic content.

title: 11+ and 13+ Tutoring for Wiltshire Students: What Parents Should Check First
excerpt: How to prepare for entrance assessments without assuming that every school uses the same tests.

sections.heading: Begin with the target school
paragraphs: The terms 11+ and 13+ describe broad ages and entry points, not a single universal paper. Entrance arrangements differ by school, and they may include English, Maths, reasoning, interviews or other tasks.
Check the school’s most recent admissions information directly for eligibility, test content, application windows and any changes. Do not rely solely on a generic 11+ workbook.

sections.heading: Build skills before speed
paragraphs: For younger learners, confidence with reading comprehension, written explanations and number fluency is a better foundation than racing through timed multiple-choice questions from day one.
Once core skills are secure, introduce the format of the actual school assessment and practise pacing. Keep sessions encouraging: the goal is to make unfamiliar questions feel manageable.

sections.heading: How a tutor supports preparation
paragraphs: A tutor can identify a child’s current strengths, select appropriately challenging material and provide feedback after attempts. For 13+ subjects, structured written responses and school-specific requirements may need greater emphasis.

title: A-Level Maths and Further Maths: When to Get Specialist Tutoring
excerpt: Spot the difference between a small topic gap and a deeper mathematical problem before it affects exam results.

sections.heading: Look beneath the latest test result
paragraphs: A low score in integration, vectors or mechanics may reflect an earlier weakness in algebra, graphs or trigonometry. More difficult worksheets rarely fix a missing prerequisite. A specialist tutor should be able to find the underlying issue and rebuild it efficiently.
Year 12 learners in particular benefit from secure algebraic methods because so much later study assumes they are fluent.

sections.heading: Understand the role of Further Maths
paragraphs: Further Maths adds demanding ideas such as complex numbers, matrices and additional pure and applied topics. Students taking both subjects need a clear timetable, not simply more independent homework.

For applicants considering mathematically intensive university courses, an experienced tutor may also help with problem-solving admissions tests such as TMUA. Check the latest official requirements for each institution.

sections.heading: Work backwards from the specification
paragraphs: Start with the relevant exam board and module content, then alternate new explanations with independent questions and timed mixed practice. Errors should be reviewed and revisited at intervals.
